issues.item: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: The threat items 'Checking Behind' and 'Back to Wall' imply a persistent interpersonal pursuit/assault-style danger (someone following me, needing surveillance of the room) that is hard to reconcile with a life-threatening motor vehicle collision unless there is additional trauma content not represented elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: 'Institutional Failure' is not a natural fit with the rest of this MVC profile: the other items center on fragmented accident memory, mistrust of self/body, and hypervigilance, but this appraisal presupposes a salient protector/institution betrayal theme that is not supported by the trauma type or other selected items.

issues.item: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event' does not connect well to the represented triggers, memory, or appraisals. For an MVC case, avoidance is more coherently focused on travel, roads, vehicles, reminders of the crash, or internal trauma cues; avoidance of prior social contacts suggests a different maintaining process that is not otherwise represented.

vignette: The asphalt had been slick with November rain when the sedan skidded across the center line, metal groaning as it pinned Kwame's torso against the steering column. He remembered the crushing weight of the hood, the smell of burnt rubber and copper, and the suffocating silence that followed the impact. When he finally clawed his way free, the emergency responders arrived hours late, their delayed paperwork and dismissive shrugs leaving his claims of negligence unanswered. To Kwame, the collision was no longer just a sudden accident; it was proof that the institutions tasked with his safety had abandoned him, and that his own limbs had betrayed him at the very moment they were needed most. The dance floor, once a space of precise control and rhythmic certainty, suddenly felt like an illusion. Every instinct he had spent forty years honing as a professional dancer now felt like a lie. In the weeks that followed, Kwame found himself trapped in a mental fog. He knew pieces of the crash-a shattered side mirror, the screech of tires-but the sequence refused to lock together. When he tried to deliberately piece the timeline, his mind went blank, leaving him with only disjointed images that refused to form a coherent story. Because he could not assemble the collision into a clear narrative, he began to question every decision he made afterward, paralyzed by a quiet self-doubt that whispered he was fundamentally broken. The fragmented nature of his recall did not fade; instead, it fed directly into his growing conviction that his mind and body were unreliable, turning a single traumatic afternoon into a permanent state of physiological betrayal. As his trust in his own faculties eroded, the world itself began to feel predatory. His conviction that institutional safeguards were hollow and his own physiology a liability pushed him toward isolation, making him systematically avoid going out or stepping into spaces where he might lose control. Believing that he had been left without protection, he stopped answering calls from his former dance troupe, telling himself he was simply tired, though he knew he was fleeing the faces of those who still moved with the grace he no longer possessed. He also found himself carefully sidestepping therapeutic discussions, his mind slipping into resistance the moment a clinician neared the mechanics of the collision or the sensations of restraint. His inability to reconstruct the event only deepened his belief that his body could not be trusted, while his growing distrust of the systems around him made deliberate memory retrieval feel dangerously futile. The constant dread of impending catastrophe and the physical compulsion to press his back against walls made leaving his apartment impossible. The incomplete, missing pieces of his recall meant that sudden noises or routine waiting periods felt indistinguishable from the moments before the crash. When he sat in his converted loft dance studio, waiting for a physical therapist or a grocery delivery to arrive, any delay triggered the certainty that something terrible was occurring. An unexpected door slam or the low rumble of a delivery truck backfiring sent him scrambling to the nearest wall, his eyes darting to ensure an escape route remained visible. The constant scanning for danger, born from his negative appraisals, made every ordinary sound feel like a precursor to impact, while his avoidance of social contacts and therapeutic exposure deprived his nervous system of any corrective reassurance. With each closed door and each avoided conversation, his threat monitoring remained permanently amplified, ensuring that the next minor delay or unstructured noise would trigger the same alarm. Now, at sixty-eight, Kwame sits on the edge of his worn rehearsal mat in the quiet loft he and his late wife had shared for three decades. The silence in the room is no longer peaceful; it is watchful. He finally scheduled this intake because the isolation has begun to starve him, and the unrelenting dread of impending catastrophe has left him too exhausted to function. What frightens him most is not the crash itself, but the certainty that he will never be safe inside his own skin again. Yet, beneath the exhaustion, he hopes this conversation might be the first place where someone finally believes him-that the failure was not his body, but the world's, and that perhaps he can learn to trust himself once more.
